candidates.whyItFits: Rhyolite mountains create landscapes that look painted—pink, yellow, and green peaks rising from black lava fields. The Laugavegur trail starts here, but even day hikers can reach Bláhnjúkur summit in 90 minutes for views across the entire highland interior.
candidates.tradeoffs: Only accessible by 4WD vehicle or highland bus from mid-June to September.
candidates.otherAttractions: Natural hot springs for soaking after hikes, Ljótipollur explosion crater, Frostastaðavatn lake

candidates.whyItFits: A geothermal field at 1000 meters elevation where steam vents emerge from rhyolite peaks. The Hveradalir valley contains dozens of hot springs and fumaroles creating an otherworldly landscape that feels more Mars than Earth.
candidates.tradeoffs: Highland road access only, weather can change rapidly at elevation.
candidates.otherAttractions: Snækollur peak hike, Ásgarður mountain hut area, natural hot pools

candidates.whyItFits: A 20-meter waterfall dropping over hexagonal basalt columns that form perfect geometric patterns. The contrast between white water and dark volcanic rock creates one of Iceland's most photogenic waterfalls, yet it sees a fraction of the crowds at Gullfoss.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires driving on highland road F26, can be muddy and rough.
candidates.otherAttractions: Nearby Hrafnabjargafoss waterfall, highland desert scenery, connection to Sprengisandur route

candidates.whyItFits: A Norwegian-style wooden town at the end of a dramatic fjord, surrounded by mountains that rise directly from sea level to 1000 meters. The drive down from the plateau offers one of Iceland's most spectacular descents.
candidates.tradeoffs: Can be foggy and rainy, limited dining options outside summer.
candidates.otherAttractions: Gufufoss waterfall hike, Skálanes nature reserve, colorful wooden church

candidates.whyItFits: A serpentine canyon carved by glacial meltwater over 9000 years, with walls reaching 100 meters high. Walking the rim trail reveals the Fjaðrá river winding through moss-covered canyon walls in perfect S-curves.
candidates.tradeoffs: Popular after appearing in a Justin Bieber video, can be crowded in summer.
candidates.otherAttractions: Nearby Eldhraun lava field, connection to highland routes, Lakagígar crater row

candidates.whyItFits: Iceland's most remote peninsula, accessible only by boat from Ísafjörður. Abandoned farms dot clifftops where Arctic foxes roam freely and seabirds nest on 500-meter cliffs. No roads, no services, just wilderness.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires serious planning—camping only, weather-dependent boat access, expensive to reach.
candidates.otherAttractions: Hornbjarg cliffs, Arctic fox watching, abandoned Hesteyri village

candidates.whyItFits: Black sand dunes meet the Atlantic with Vestrahorn mountain as backdrop. The contrast between flowing sand patterns and jagged peaks creates constantly changing compositions, especially dramatic during storms or under northern lights.
candidates.tradeoffs: Small entrance fee to access the peninsula, can be very windy.
candidates.otherAttractions: Viking village film set, lighthouse, seal watching

candidates.whyItFits: Volcanic islands where the 1973 eruption buried a third of the town under lava. Eldfell crater still steams, and you can walk through neighborhoods where houses emerge from hardened lava flows. The newest land in Iceland, still being shaped.
candidates.tradeoffs: Ferry dependent, can be cancelled in rough weather.
candidates.otherAttractions: Puffin colonies at Stórhöfði, Eldheimar volcano museum, Elephant Rock sea stack

candidates.whyItFits: Iceland's third-highest waterfall drops 128 meters over cliff faces striped with red clay layers—geological history written in stone. The 45-minute hike passes Litlanesfoss, where basalt columns frame a smaller waterfall.
candidates.tradeoffs: Moderate uphill hike required, can be icy in winter.
candidates.otherAttractions: Litlanesfoss basalt columns, views over Lagarfljót lake, connection to East Fjords

candidates.whyItFits: 3,000-year-old volcanic crater with a turquoise lake at the bottom, offering a different perspective on Iceland's geological formation than the more famous geysers nearby.
candidates.tradeoffs: Small entrance fee required and can get crowded during peak hours.

candidates.whyItFits: Waterfall framed by hexagonal basalt columns that inspired Reykjavík's Hallgrímskirkja church design, accessible via moderate hike from Skaftafell visitor center.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires 1.5-hour round-trip hike on sometimes muddy trails.

candidates.whyItFits: Small island accessible by boat where Irish monks lived before Norse settlement, now home to thousands of puffins during summer months.
candidates.tradeoffs: Boat trips weather-dependent and only operate during summer season.

candidates.whyItFits: Active volcanic system with colorful crater lake and geothermal power station, showing Iceland's ongoing geological activity beyond the tourist-focused areas.
candidates.tradeoffs: Road can be rough and area may be restricted during periods of volcanic activity.

candidates.whyItFits: Narrow ravine you can walk into between towering cliff walls, created by a legendary giant throwing a boulder, offering intimate geological experience.
candidates.tradeoffs: Can be slippery and requires scrambling over rocks, not suitable for all fitness levels.

candidates.whyItFits: Largest lake on Reykjanes Peninsula with geothermal activity beneath causing water levels to fluctuate dramatically - the lake partially drained in 2000 after earthquakes opened fissures in the lakebed.
candidates.tradeoffs: Can be windy and desolate even by Icelandic standards.

candidates.whyItFits: Active geothermal field with bubbling mud pools and sulfur springs, less crowded than other geothermal sites but equally dramatic.
candidates.tradeoffs: Strong sulfur smell and unstable ground require staying on marked paths.

candidates.whyItFits: Small island accessible by ferry from Reykjavík harbor, home to Yoko Ono's Imagine Peace Tower and Iceland's oldest stone building from 1755.
candidates.tradeoffs: Ferry schedule limits visit duration and weather can cancel service.

candidates.whyItFits: Green valley within Reykjavík city limits with hiking trails and small waterfalls, where locals go to escape urban life without leaving town.
candidates.tradeoffs: Not dramatic by Icelandic standards, more about peaceful walking than spectacular views.

candidates.whyItFits: Twin lighthouses on the tip of Reykjanes Peninsula with views across Faxaflói Bay to Reykjavík and Mount Esja.
candidates.tradeoffs: Often very windy and can be difficult to access in bad weather.

candidates.whyItFits: Sacred mountain in Icelandic folklore where locals believe three wishes will be granted if you climb it in silence and don't look back.
candidates.tradeoffs: Short hike with modest views compared to other Icelandic peaks.

candidates.whyItFits: Small island connected to Stykkishólmur by a causeway, topped with a lighthouse offering panoramic views of Breiðafjörður Bay and its countless islands.
candidates.tradeoffs: Very exposed to wind and weather with limited shelter.

candidates.whyItFits: Hidden waterfall partially concealed behind a rock face, requiring a short wade through a stream to reach the viewing area behind the falls.
candidates.tradeoffs: Getting close means getting wet, and the narrow canyon can feel claustrophobic.

candidates.whyItFits: Lesser-known waterfall a short hike from Skógafoss where you can walk behind the falls without the crowds.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires a muddy 15-minute hike and can be slippery near the falls.

candidates.whyItFits: Smaller waterfall on the same river system as Gullfoss, with a fish ladder built in 1947 to help salmon migrate upstream.
candidates.tradeoffs: Much less dramatic than nearby Gullfoss and can feel anticlimactic in comparison.

candidates.whyItFits: Waterfall framed by distinctive basalt columns that create a natural amphitheater, considered one of Iceland's most photogenic falls.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires a rough 4WD road to access and can be impassable in winter.

candidates.whyItFits: Horseshoe-shaped waterfall 2km downstream from Dettifoss, where the Jökulsá á Fjöllum river cuts through columnar basalt formations.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires additional hiking on rough terrain.

candidates.whyItFits: Multi-tiered waterfall 1km upstream from Dettifoss, creating a series of cascades across the river width.
candidates.tradeoffs: Less dramatic than its famous neighbor.

candidates.whyItFits: The actual walking path through the rift valley where the Althing assembly met from 930 AD, between the American and Eurasian tectonic plates.
candidates.tradeoffs: Can be crowded during peak hours.

candidates.whyItFits: Waterfall within Þingvellir where the Öxará river was deliberately diverted in the 10th century to provide fresh water for the parliament gatherings.
candidates.tradeoffs: Modest scale compared to Iceland's major waterfalls.

candidates.whyItFits: Active geyser that erupts every 5-10 minutes to heights of 15-20 meters, located in the same geothermal field as the original Geysir.
candidates.tradeoffs: Often confused with Geysir itself by visitors.

candidates.whyItFits: Twin hot springs with contrasting colors - one crystal clear, one milky blue from silica deposits - in the Haukadalur geothermal valley.
candidates.tradeoffs: Easy to overlook among the more active features.

candidates.whyItFits: Rhyolite mountain ridge that creates the geothermal activity at Hverir, with hiking trails offering views over the sulfur fields and Lake Mývatn.
candidates.tradeoffs: Steep climb required for best viewpoints.

candidates.whyItFits: Geothermal power station and diatomite quarry where you can see industrial use of the same forces that create Hverir's mud pots.
candidates.tradeoffs: Industrial setting lacks natural beauty.

candidates.whyItFits: Forested peninsula extending into Lake Mývatn with walking trails through birch woods and views of the pseudocraters.
candidates.tradeoffs: Midges can be intense during summer months.

candidates.whyItFits: Pseudocrater field formed when lava flowed over wetlands, creating steam explosions that left circular formations around Lake Mývatn.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires walking on uneven lava terrain.

candidates.whyItFits: Geothermal area with colorful mud pools and fumaroles, showing the same volcanic activity that shapes the Reykjanes Peninsula.
candidates.tradeoffs: Strong sulfur smell can be overwhelming.

candidates.whyItFits: Lake that lost a third of its water after the 2000 earthquakes opened fissures in its bottom, demonstrating ongoing geological activity.
candidates.tradeoffs: Can appear unremarkable without knowing its recent history.

candidates.whyItFits: Outlet glacier from Vatnajökull with accessible terminus for close glacier viewing and ice cave formations in winter.
candidates.tradeoffs: Glacier has retreated significantly in recent decades.

candidates.whyItFits: Mountain peaks offering challenging day hikes with views over Vatnajökull glacier and the Skaftafell area.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires mountaineering experience and proper equipment.

candidates.whyItFits: Glacial lagoon formed more recently than Jökulsárlón, showing the rapid retreat of Breiðamerkurjökull glacier.
candidates.tradeoffs: Smaller and less dramatic than its famous neighbor.

candidates.whyItFits: Black sand dunes and beach with views of Vestrahorn mountain, offering a different perspective on the southeastern coast.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires small entrance fee to private land.

candidates.whyItFits: Black sand plain between the two glacier lagoons where icebergs sometimes strand, creating a different perspective on glacier calving.
candidates.tradeoffs: Weather-dependent visibility and iceberg presence.

candidates.whyItFits: Hidden waterfall behind Skógafoss requiring a 15-minute walk, offers the behind-the-falls experience without crowds.
candidates.tradeoffs: Muddy trail conditions and river crossing required.

candidates.whyItFits: Isolated cliff formation rising from black sand plains, named for one of Iceland's first settlers and offering 360-degree coastal views.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires driving on rough gravel roads.

candidates.whyItFits: Natural stone arch carved by waves, accessible via coastal walking path from Arnarstapi village.
candidates.tradeoffs: Can be missed if weather obscures the coastline.

candidates.whyItFits: Lava tube containing year-round ice formations and sculptures, accessible only by guided tour from the Mývatn area.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires advance booking and specialized tour operator.

candidates.whyItFits: Recent lava flows from 1970s-80s eruptions create a moonscape of hardened rock formations you can walk across.
candidates.tradeoffs: Landscape can feel barren.

candidates.whyItFits: Fossil-rich cliffs where 2-15 million year old marine shells are embedded in the rock layers, visible from coastal walking paths.
candidates.tradeoffs: Requires geological interest to appreciate.

candidates.whyItFits: Red pseudocraters formed when lava flowed over wetlands, creating distinctive rust-colored mounds in the landscape.
candidates.tradeoffs: Subtle feature that some may find unremarkable.

candidates.whyItFits: Series of small waterfalls cascading down the mountainside directly behind Kirkjufell, visible from the main viewing area.
candidates.tradeoffs: Modest compared to major waterfalls.

candidates.whyItFits: Small volcanic crater with metal stairs leading to the rim, offering views across the Snæfellsnes lava fields toward the glacier.
candidates.tradeoffs: Brief stop with limited time needed.

candidates.whyItFits: Reconstructed 19th-century fishing station on Bolungarvík's coast showing how crews lived through winter storms when boats couldn't return to harbor.
candidates.tradeoffs: Small scale - you'll see everything in 30 minutes.

candidates.whyItFits: Red sand beach stretching 10km along Látrabjarg peninsula - Iceland's rare warm-toned coastline created by crushed scallop shells.
candidates.tradeoffs: Rough gravel road access requires careful driving.

candidates.whyItFits: Medieval scholar Snorri Sturluson's estate where he wrote the Prose Edda in the 1220s - the primary source for Norse mythology we know today.
candidates.tradeoffs: Mostly foundations and interpretation rather than standing structures.

candidates.whyItFits: Spring water emerges directly from lava rock face across 900 meters, creating dozens of small waterfalls that seem to flow from solid stone.
candidates.tradeoffs: Popular with tour groups during summer midday hours.

candidates.whyItFits: Archaeological remains of a 10th-century longhouse discovered under downtown Reykjavík, built around the time of Iceland's first permanent settlement.
candidates.tradeoffs: Indoor museum experience rather than outdoor exploration.

placeActivities.name: Place to stay overnight
placeActivities.description: Cities and towns you flagged as overnight stays. These anchor the trip's geography — they're where you sleep and the bases for day trips.

placeActivities.name: Drive the Ring Road
placeActivities.description: Iceland's Route 1 circles the entire island, connecting all major natural landmarks and providing access to the country's most dramatic landscapes.

placeActivities.name: Chase the Northern Lights
placeActivities.description: Aurora borealis appears on clear nights from September through March, best viewed away from light pollution.
placeActivities.conditionNote: Clear skies and solar activity determine visibility

placeActivities.name: Walk to waterfalls
placeActivities.description: Iceland's waterfalls range from roadside cascades to multi-hour hikes, each shaped by the island's glacial and volcanic geology.

placeActivities.name: Explore volcanic landscapes
placeActivities.description: Active geothermal areas, lava fields, and volcanic formations show Iceland's position on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

placeActivities.name: Walk on glaciers and ice
placeActivities.description: Vatnajökull's outlet glaciers create lagoons, icebergs, and accessible ice formations along the southeast coast.

placeActivities.name: Stand at dramatic coastlines
placeActivities.description: Black sand beaches, basalt columns, and sea stacks formed by volcanic activity meeting the North Atlantic.

placeActivities.name: Soak in geothermal waters
placeActivities.description: Natural hot springs and purpose-built lagoons use Iceland's geothermal energy for bathing year-round.

placeActivities.name: Drive the Golden Circle
placeActivities.description: The classic day circuit from Reykjavík connects Þingvellir, Geysir, and Gullfoss in a 300km loop.

placeActivities.name: Explore the East Fjords
placeActivities.description: Iceland's oldest geological formations create deep fjords and mountain landscapes distinct from the volcanic south.

placeActivities.name: Drive the Diamond Circle
placeActivities.description: North Iceland's answer to the Golden Circle connects Húsavík, Ásbyrgi, Dettifoss, and Lake Mývatn.

placeActivities.name: Experience Reykjavík culture
placeActivities.description: The world's northernmost capital combines Nordic design, literary tradition, and a compact downtown walkable in an afternoon.

placeActivities.name: Taste Icelandic food
placeActivities.description: Traditional preservation methods, modern Nordic cuisine, and ingredients shaped by isolation and climate.

placeActivities.name: Explore Snæfellsnes Peninsula
placeActivities.description: Called 'Iceland in miniature' for containing glaciers, lava fields, fishing villages, and coastal cliffs in one peninsula.

placeActivities.name: Visit the Monument to the Unknown Bureaucrat
placeActivities.description: Magnús Tómasson's 1994 sculpture in Reykjavík comments on modern administrative life through an anonymous figure tied to his desk.

placeActivities.name: Other stays to consider
placeActivities.description: Consider these additional bases for better geographic coverage and reduced driving distances.

placeActivities.name: Max-suggested additions, in the shape of your list
placeActivities.description: Max read your existing picks as a signal of taste and added these. Check the ones that fit; ignore the rest.

placeActivities.name: Near-by enrichment
placeActivities.description: Nearby sights and activities tied to the places already in your Discovery. Each one is anchored to a place you've listed.
